text:
Recent work supports probing history dependence while separating sensitivity from preference interpretation. [Measuring Recency Bias (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722) quantifies excessive emphasis on recent interactions and reports improved recommendation performance after mitigation; stronger recency dependence is therefore not automatically desirable. [Demystifying Sequential Recommendations (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03606) searches for minimal discrete history edits that change recommendations, evaluating targeted and untargeted counterfactuals across three datasets and models. [CoDeR+ (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3778863) models demand drift and interest confounding, providing motivation for distinguishing short-term changes from stable interests, although its causal conclusions depend on its modeling assumptions.

Suggested diagnostic synthesis: pair deletion of recent coherent activity with equal-size random and older-history deletions; compare recent-only truncation against equally long historical windows; shuffle within windows while preserving item membership to isolate order sensitivity. Measure original-target score/rank changes and top-10 overlap on fixed candidates, reporting paired differences, repeated random-control variability, and user-level bootstrap confidence intervals. These are proposed design choices, not an established protocol from the cited papers. The [2024 faithfulness survey](https://aclanthology.org/2024.cl-2.6/) warns that erasure can introduce out-of-distribution artifacts: use small edit budgets, preserve valid sequence formatting, and compare deletion, truncation, and local shuffling before interpreting agreement. For BERT4Rec, retain left padding and appended-mask inference; removing an event must not accidentally alter readout logic. Such probes establish dependence of a fixed model’s outputs on supplied history—not actual ownership, fulfilled needs, purchase intent, or causally identified preference drift.
